## Introduction

Sexual objectification (SO) is a pervasive feature of women's everyday experiences, reflecting broader gendered patterns in how women are perceived, evaluated, and treated. SO occurs when individuals – particularly women – are regarded primarily in terms of their physical appearance and sexual desirability rather than as whole people with unique thoughts, identities, and agency (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997; Nussbaum, 1995; Pecini et al., 2023). These experiences can manifest through interpersonal interactions, including unwanted staring, sexually suggestive comments, catcalling, and unwanted sexual advances, as well as through broader cultural representations that emphasize women's appearance and sexual desirability (Kozee et al., 2007; Ward, 2016). Importantly, sexual objectification is not limited to isolated incidents but represents a recurring feature of women's social environments (Holland et al., 2017).

Objectification theory (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997) provides a framework for understanding the psychological consequences of these experiences. Repeated exposure to sexually objectifying treatment can encourage women to internalize an outsider perspective of their bodies, contributing to self-objectification, body surveillance, body shame, and appearance-related anxiety (Moradi & Huang, 2008; Szymanski et al., 2011). However, the implications of sexual objectification extend beyond women's perceptions of their appearance. Experiences of objectification can also contribute to concerns about personal safety, physical vulnerability, and the possibility of unwanted or threatening interactions (Calogero et al., 2021). In turn, these concerns may influence how women navigate their social environments and respond to potentially threatening situations.

Calogero and colleagues (2021) conceptualized personal safety anxiety as a diffuse sense of apprehension and vigilance concerning potential threats to one's physical safety and personal boundaries. Their research demonstrated that experiences of sexual objectification were associated with greater personal safety anxiety, which subsequently contributed to restrictions in women's spatial autonomy. These findings suggest that sexual objectification may influence not only how women perceive themselves, but also how safe they feel navigating everyday environments. Given the potential implications of these experiences for women's autonomy and well-being, identifying factors associated with the propensity to experience personal safety anxiety and vigilance represents an important direction for further research.

Although sexual objectification may contribute to heightened concerns about personal safety, women may differ in how they interpret and respond to these experiences. One potentially relevant individual difference is benevolent sexism (BS). According to ambivalent sexism theory (Glick & Fiske, 1996), sexism encompasses both hostile and benevolent attitudes toward women. Whereas hostile sexism involves explicitly negative attitudes and stereotypes, benevolent sexism consists of subjectively positive attitudes that idealize women while simultaneously reinforcing traditional gender roles and gender inequality. Notably, benevolent sexism positions women as inherently vulnerable, morally superior, and deserving of male protection, framing men as protectors and women as dependent recipients of protection (Glick & Fiske, 1996).

Despite its seemingly favourable presentation, benevolent sexism can reinforce gendered expectations and power differences. For example, beliefs that women require protection may contribute to the normalization of women's perceived vulnerability or the expectation of men’s protection, potentially shaping how they interpret experiences that threaten their personal safety. Extant research has demonstrated that benevolent sexist attitudes toward women can have consequential implications for women's responses to gender inequality, including reduced engagement in collective action (Becker & Wright, 2011). Additionally, individuals may be less likely to recognize benevolent sexism as discriminatory because of its comparatively positive and complimentary façade (Hopkins-Doyle et al., 2019).

Considering these implications, benevolent sexism may be particularly relevant to understanding individual differences in women's personal safety anxiety following sexually objectifying experiences. Specifically, women who strongly endorse benevolent sexism may be more likely to interpret objectifying experiences through a framework of flattery or protective paternalism. As such, these beliefs may limit how threatening women perceive such experiences to be, thereby altering the association between sexual objectification and personal safety anxiety. Although previous research has established an association between sexual objectification and personal safety anxiety (Calogero et al., 2021), less is understood about whether this relationship varies according to women's endorsement of benevolent sexism.

The present study examined the association between the frequency of women’s sexual objectification experiences and their personal safety anxiety, with particular attention to the potential moderating role of benevolent sexism. Specifically, this project investigated whether more frequent experiences of sexual objectification were associated with greater personal safety anxiety and whether the strength of this association differed according to women's endorsement of benevolent sexism. Understanding these relationships may contribute to a more comprehensive account of the psychological implications of everyday objectification and the individual differences that may shape women's experiences of personal safety.

Two main hypotheses guided the analysis:

- Hypothesis 1: More frequent experiences of sexual objectification will be positively associated with women’s personal safety anxiety.
- Hypothesis 2: Benevolent sexism will moderate the association between experiences of sexual objectification and personal safety anxiety, such that the positive association will be weaker among women reporting higher levels of benevolent sexism.

## Methods
```{r}
#| output: false
library(tidyverse)
library(naniar)
library(car)
library(gt)
library(openxlsx)
library(dplyr)
library(psych)
library(performance)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(lmtest)
library(emmeans)
library(ggeffects)
library(sandwich)
library(patchwork)

# Loading dataset
my_data <- read.xlsx("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/agraha89/graham-capstone/main/Dataset.xlsx", sheet = 1)

# Investigating MCAR and percentage missing for each item --> Low missingness and non-significant MCAR test help justify item-level mean imputation for scale scoring
mcar <- mcar_test(my_data)

Item_Missingness <- colMeans(is.na(my_data[, c(paste0("SO", 1:11),
                             paste0("BS", 1:6),
                             paste0("PSA", 1:8))])) * 100 
  
Item_Missingness_Value <- max(Item_Missingness)

#### Scoring Scales ####
moderation_analysis.df <- my_data
v_keys <- list(
  Sexual_Objectification_Experiences = c("SO1", "SO2", "SO3", "SO4", "SO5", "SO6", "SO7", "SO8", "SO9", "SO10", "SO11"),
  Benevolent_Sexism = c("BS1", "BS2", "BS3", "BS4", "BS5", "BS6"),
  Safety_Anxiety = c("PSA1", "PSA2", "PSA3", "PSA4", "PSA5", "PSA6", "PSA7", "PSA8")) 

# Scoring Sexual Objectification Frequency Scale
SO_scores <- scoreItems(
  v_keys["Sexual_Objectification_Experiences"],
  moderation_analysis.df,
  totals = F,
  min = 1,
  max = 5,
  impute = "mean") # Using mean imputation to handle missing item values

# Scoring Benevolent Sexism Subscale
BS_scores <- scoreItems(
  v_keys["Benevolent_Sexism"],
  moderation_analysis.df,
  totals = F,
  min = 1,
  max = 5,
  impute = "mean")

# Scoring Personal Safety Anxiety Scale
PSA_scores <- scoreItems(
  v_keys["Safety_Anxiety"],
  moderation_analysis.df,
  totals = F,
  min = 1,
  max = 7,
  impute = "mean")

# Creating and combining dataframes of scores
SO_scores.df <- as.data.frame(SO_scores$scores)
BS_scores.df <- as.data.frame(BS_scores$scores)
PSA_scores.df <- as.data.frame(PSA_scores$scores)
allscores.df <- cbind(SO_scores.df, BS_scores.df, PSA_scores.df) |> 
  mutate(SO_c = Sexual_Objectification_Experiences - mean(Sexual_Objectification_Experiences),
         BS_c = Benevolent_Sexism - mean(Benevolent_Sexism),
         SA_c = Safety_Anxiety - mean(Safety_Anxiety))

# Creating demographics dataframe
demographics.df <- my_data |> 
  select(Religiosity, Political.Orientation, Age, `LGBTQ2S+.Identity`)

# Examining distributions
Rel_Distribution <- ggplot(demographics.df, aes(x = Religiosity)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 7, # Note fewer bins due to limited response options (compared to outcomes scale measures' composite scores)
    fill = "#669BBC",
    color = "white",
    alpha = 0.8,
    na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Degree of Religiosity",
       y = "Number of Participants") +

        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5))

PO_Distribution <- ggplot(demographics.df, aes(x = Political.Orientation)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 7,
    fill = "#669BBC",
    color = "white",
    alpha = 0.8,
    na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Political Orientation (Higher = Right-Leaning)",
       y = "Number of Participants") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5))

Age_Distribution <- ggplot(demographics.df, aes(x = Age)) +

    fill = "#669BBC",

LGBTQ2S_Distribution <- ggplot(demographics.df, aes(x = `LGBTQ2S+.Identity`)) +

    bins = 2,

N <- nrow(allscores.df) # Creating an object to capture sample size

# Creating new dataframe with descriptive stats for continuous demographic measures

# Assigning labels to variables and selecting on relevant stats for the table

Summary <- Summary |>

m_SO <- round(Summary$mean[1], 2)
sd_SO <- round(Summary$sd[1], 2)

sd_BS <- round(Summary$sd[2], 2)

sd_PSA <- round(Summary$sd[3], 2)

# Examining distributions of continuous measures
```

#### Data Source and Participants
The current project used an existing clean, anonymized dataset containing participants' responses to measures of sexual objectification frequency, benevolent sexism, personal safety anxiety, and relevant demographic characteristics. Data were collected in early 2026 as part of an undergraduate thesis project at Western University (Desmarais, 2026; WREB Approval #128042) examining whether various emotional responses mediated the association between the frequency of experiencing daily sexist events and resistance to sexual objectification. Additional data (including variables analyzed here) were collected as part of this project, providing a comprehensive dataset of variables related to women’s experiences of and attitudes toward sexism and objectification. The dataset for the current project is available through an Excel workbook hosted in its corresponding GitHub repository. As noted in the repository's `README.md` file, the unit of observation is the individual participant, with each row representing one respondent and each column representing an item-level response or demographic characteristic. In accordance with the ethics agreement terms, the principal investigator approved the sharing of the reduced, anonymized dataset used for the current project. 

Data were originally collected from 358 undergraduate women using Western University’s Psychology research participation pool (SONA). After excluding duplicates and poor-response cases (i.e., straight-lining, failed attention checks, incomplete responses, low reCAPTCHA score), the final sample consisted of `r N` self-identified women (*M*~age~ = `r m_Age`, *SD* = `r sd_Age`). On average, participants reported low levels of religiosity (*M* = `r m_Rel`, *SD* = `r sd_Rel`) and identified as politically left-leaning to centrist (*M* = `r m_PO`, *SD* = `r sd_PO`). `r LGBTQ2S_Proportion`% identified as members of the LGBTQ2S+ community.

#### Measures, Data Preparation, and Missing Data Handling

As presented in the table below, the main variables of interest were women's frequency of experiencing sexual objectification (SO; predictor), benevolent sexist attitudes (BS; moderator), and personal safety anxiety and vigilance (PSA; outcome). Whereas the measures of benevolent sexism (α = `r round(BS_scores$alpha, 2)`; Glick & Whitehead, 2010) and personal safety anxiety (α = `r round(PSA_scores$alpha, 2)`; Calogero et al., 2021) were taken directly from validated scales, the measure of sexual objectification frequency (α = `r round(SO_scores$alpha, 2)`) was created by compiling 11 relevant items from three relevant validated scales (Cary et al., 2024; Kozee et al., 2007; Swim et al., 1998). Items were averaged to compute composite scale scores, reverse-coding where applicable. Higher scores indicated more frequent sexual objectification experiences, higher benevolent sexism attitudes, and higher personal safety anxiety and vigilance, respectively. Given low item missingness (largest value = `r round(Item_Missingness_Value, 2)`%) and a non-significant MCAR test (χ²(`r round(mcar$df, 2)`) = `r round(mcar$statistic, 2)`, *p* = `r round(mcar$p.value, 3)`), item-level mean imputation was used to retain the available participant responses while minimizing the loss of observations. Details of the key variables' items and scoring are available in the provided `README.md` file hosted in this project's GitHub repository. 

| Variable    | Description                                                    |
|-------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `SO`        | **Predictor:** Frequency of sexual objectification experiences |
| `BS`        | **Moderator:** Benevolent sexism attitudes/endorsement         |
| `PSA`       | **Outcome:** Personal safety anxiety and vigilance             |

#### Analytic Strategy
A series of nested linear regression models was estimated to examine the association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety, and assess whether benevolent sexism moderated this relationship. Mean-centred versions of the scale scores were computed and used for these models. Linear regression was selected because the outcome variable was a continuous composite score and the primary objective was to examine the associations between continuous predictors and personal safety anxiety. Note that some researchers may argue that an ordinal model is better suited to the data, as the variables were measured using Likert scales. Linear models are used here because the composite scores behave as quasi-continuous and because interaction effects are simpler to specify and interpret. Additional analyses beyond the scope of the current project may find value in comparing the results of linear and ordinal regression models. 

| Model | Formula | Research rationale |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| Null | `PSA ~ 1` | Baseline model |
| Predictor-Only | `PSA ~ SO` | Frequency of sexual objectification experiences predicts safety anxiety |
| Interaction | `PSA ~ SO + BS + SO * BS` | Interaction explains additional variation |

As outlined in the table above, a series of nested regression models was estimated to determine whether sexual objectification frequency and benevolent sexism explained meaningful variance in personal safety anxiety and whether their interaction improved model performance. The first model was an intercept-only model, providing a baseline against which subsequent improvements in model fit could be evaluated. The second model included sexual objectification frequency as the sole predictor of personal safety anxiety. The third model added benevolent sexism to determine whether it explained additional variance beyond sexual objectification frequency. Finally, the fourth model included the interaction between sexual objectification frequency and benevolent sexism to evaluate the proposed moderation effect.

Model comparisons were conducted using nested-model F-tests and evaluating changes in explained variance (ΔR²), adjusted R², and RMSE. These statistics provided complementary information regarding whether additional predictors meaningfully improved performance relative to the increased complexity of each model. AIC was also examined as a supplementary indicator of relative model fit.

Regression diagnostics were examined to evaluate the assumptions underlying linear regression analyses. These included assessments of linearity, residual normality, homogeneity of variance, multicollinearity, and influential observations.

Finally, simple slopes were estimated to examine the association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety at low, average, and high levels of benevolent sexism (−1 SD, the mean, and +1 SD, respectively). These analyses were used to facilitate interpretation of the interaction model and assess whether the association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety differed across levels of benevolent sexism. A sensitivity analysis (see Appendix) was also conducted after excluding observations flagged during preliminary diagnostic assessments to evaluate the stability of the primary regression findings.

```{r}
SO_by_PSA <- cor.test(allscores.df$Sexual_Objectification_Experiences, allscores.df$Safety_Anxiety, method = "pearson")
```

After examining the scales' descriptive statistics (below) for notable patterns and issues of concern, zero-order Pearson correlations and scatterplots were examined to provide an initial evaluation of the relationships between the key variables. This examination revealed suprisingly weak associations, with the largest correlation demonstrating a significant and positive association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety, *r*(`r SO_by_PSA$parameter`) = `r round(SO_by_PSA$estimate, 2)`, *p* `r ifelse(SO_by_PSA$p.value < .001, "< .001", paste("=", round(SO_by_PSA$p.value, 3)))`. This noted, the associations (i.e., not the residuals) appear approximately linear, although the weak correlations make it difficult to discern whether any observations are potential outliers.

#### Model Comparison and Selection

```{r}
## Intercept-only Model
mod0 <- lm(SA_c ~ 1, data = allscores.df)

# Single-predictor model
mod1 <- lm(SA_c ~ SO_c, data = allscores.df)

# Two-predictor model
mod2 <- lm(SA_c ~ SO_c + BS_c, data = allscores.df)

# Interaction model
mod3 <- lm(SA_c ~ SO_c + BS_c + SO_c * BS_c, data = allscores.df)

# Running nested model comparisons
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

nested.f.tests <- tests |>
  select(Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`) |> # Selecting relevant stats to keep
  rename("Residual DF" = Res.Df,
         "Change in Df" = Df,
         "Nested F" = F,
         "Nested p" = `Pr(>F)`) |> 
  mutate(`Nested p` = ifelse(`Nested p` < 0.001,
                             "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", `Nested p`))) |> 
  mutate(Model = c("Intercept-only", "M1: SO Experiences", "M2: + Benevolent Sexism", "M3: + Interaction")) |> # Adding informative model labels
  relocate(Model, .before = 1)

# Extracting overall model performance
glance0 <- glance(mod0)
glance1 <- glance(mod1)
glance2 <- glance(mod2)
glance3 <- glance(mod3)

# Combining individual model performance metrics into one dataframe
glances <- rbind(glance0,
                 glance1,
                 glance2,
                 glance3) |> 
  mutate(Model = c("Intercept-only", "M1: SO Experiences", "M2: + Benevolent Sexism", "M3: + Interaction")) |> 
  relocate(Model, .before = 1)

# Creating gt table
nested.f.tests.table <- gt(nested.f.tests) |> 
  fmt_number(columns = c("Nested F"), decimals = 2) |> 
  cols_align(align = "left")

## Combining nested tests and model performance
comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = glances,
  nested.f.tests)

# Selecting relevant statistics for table
comparison_table <- comparison_table |>
  mutate(Delta.R2 = Model.r.squared - lag(Model.r.squared),
         RMSE = c(sqrt(mean(residuals(mod0)^2)),
                  sqrt(mean(residuals(mod1)^2)),
                  sqrt(mean(residuals(mod2)^2)),
                  sqrt(mean(residuals(mod3)^2)))) |>
  select(Model.Model,
         Model.r.squared,
         Delta.R2,
         Model.adj.r.squared,
         RMSE,
         Model.statistic,
         Model.df,
         "Residual DF",
         "Change in Df",
         "Nested F",
         "Nested p",
         Model.AIC)

## Displaying combined model-comparison table
comparison_table |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(
    Model.r.squared,
    Model.adj.r.squared,
    RMSE,
    Model.statistic,
    Delta.R2,
    "Nested F"),
    decimals = 2) |>
  sub_missing(columns = c(Delta.R2, Model.statistic, Model.df, "Change in Df", "Nested F", "Nested p"),
              missing_text = "—") |> 
  cols_label(Model.Model = "Model",
             Model.r.squared = "R²",
             Model.adj.r.squared = "Adjusted R²",
             RMSE = "RMSE",
             Model.statistic = "F",
             Model.df = "df",
             Delta.R2 = "ΔR²",
             "Change in Df" = "Nested df",
             Model.AIC = "AIC") |> 
  cols_move(columns = Delta.R2,
            after = "Residual DF") |> 
  cols_move(columns = `Nested F`,
            after = Delta.R2) |> 
  tab_header(title = "Nested Model Comparisons")

```

As evidenced in the table above, the model with sexual objectification frequency as the sole predictor explained only `r round(comparison_table$Model.r.squared[2] * 100, 1)`% of the variance in the outcome. Compared with the intercept-only model, adding sexual objectification frequency significantly improved model fit, *F*(`r comparison_table[["Change in Df"]][2]`, `r comparison_table[["Residual DF"]][2]`) = `r round(comparison_table[["Nested F"]][2], 2)`, *p* `r comparison_table[["Nested p"]][2]`. The RMSE decreased from `r round(comparison_table$RMSE[1], 2)` in the intercept-only model to `r round(comparison_table$RMSE[2], 2)`, indicating a modest improvement in prediction.

Adding benevolent sexism in the subsequent model did not significantly improve model fit, *F*(`r comparison_table[["Change in Df"]][3]`, `r comparison_table[["Residual DF"]][3]`) = `r round(comparison_table[["Nested F"]][3], 2)`, *p* = `r comparison_table[["Nested p"]][3]`. The additional predictor explained negligible variance beyond sexual objectification frequency, with R² remaining unchanged. Furthermore, RMSE also remained unchanged.

Finally, the interaction model was examined to determine whether the association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety varied according to benevolent sexism. The addition of the interaction did not significantly improve model performance, *F*(`r comparison_table[["Change in Df"]][4]`, `r comparison_table[["Residual DF"]][4]`) = `r round(comparison_table[["Nested F"]][4], 2)`, *p* = `r comparison_table[["Nested p"]][4]`. The overall model explained `r round(comparison_table$Model.r.squared[4] * 100, 1)`% of the variance in personal safety anxiety. Adjusted R² did not change and AIC changed negligibly from `r round(comparison_table$Model.AIC[3], 2)` to `r round(comparison_table$Model.AIC[4], 2)`.

Taken together, the model comparisons suggest that the single-predictor model provided the most parsimonious model supported by the observed data, whereas adding benevolent sexism and the interaction term did not meaningfully improve the model's explanatory or predictive performance after accounting for model complexity. Nonetheless, as the moderation analysis remained the primary purpose of this project, diagnostic checks and interaction tests were subsequently undertaken to examine the patterns of effects.

#### Diagnostic Checks

```{r}
#| output: false
check_collinearity(mod3) # Low correlation --> Multicollinearity not a concern

outlier <- outlierTest(mod3) # No Studentized residuals with Bonferroni p < 0.05

# Modelling standardized residuals to see what proportion have sample/theoretical quantiles +/- 2SDs
std_res <- rstandard(mod3)

percent_above_2_quantiles <- mean(abs(std_res) > 2) * 100 # 5.3% --> Within normal, so residual normality is not a concern here
```
Diagnostic assessments were conducted for the interaction model to evaluate the appropriateness of the regression estimates and associated statistical tests. As shown below, the diagnostic plots suggested some potential deviations from the assumptions of linear regression, including slight curvature in the tail-ends of the residual normality and homogeneity-of-variance assessments. However, there was no substantial evidence of multicollinearity, and the observations did not appear to exceed the relevant Cook's distance contours. No significant residual outliers were identified; the largest observation was not statistically significant (r~student~ = `r round(outlier$rstudent[1], 2)`, *p*~Bonferroni~ = `r round(outlier$bonf.p[1], 3)`).

Although several observations were initially flagged during preliminary diagnostic assessments (i.e., `plot(mod3)`), further examination did not indicate that any single observation exerted an excessive influence on the fitted model. Approximately `r round(percent_above_2_quantiles, 1)`% of standardized residuals exceeded ±2, which did not suggest a meaningful departure from expected residual behaviour.
```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-width: 8
check_model(mod3)

# Evaluate Regression Diagnostics
#plot(mod3) plots suggest that observations 11, 33, 48, 83, and 193 may bias the regression analysis
## check_model plots suggest no influential observations (i.e., all within contour lines), but slight curvature at tail ends of normality of residuals plot and at left tail of homogeneity of variance plot
```
Overall, the diagnostic plots suggest that the interaction model is a relatively reasonable description of the data. Given the potential for heteroscedasticity to bias the findings, however, heteroscedasticity-consistent HC3 robust standard errors were used when evaluating the interaction model. This estimator adjusts standard errors to provide more robust inferences when the assumption of constant residual variance may not be satisfied. As an additional check, a sensitivity model that excluded five observations flagged as potentially influential by `plot(mod3)` was conducted. As the findings did not substantively alter the conclusions, the top-line results of this additional analysis are included in the appendix.

#### Interaction Model with HC3 Estimator

```{r}
#| output: false
# Reporting regression results for original model with HC3 SE estimate
coefficient_results <- tidy(coeftest(mod3, vcov = vcovHC(mod3, type = "HC3")),
                                        conf.int = TRUE,
                                        conf.level = 0.95)

# Simple slopes: Looking at influence of sexual objectification frequency at specific values of benevolent sexism
# Pick the probing values: low (-1 SD), average (mean) and high (+1 SD) benevolent sexism
BS_mean <- mean(allscores.df$BS_c, na.rm = TRUE)
BS_sd <- sd(allscores.df$BS_c, na.rm = TRUE)
BS_values <- BS_mean + c(-1, 0, 1) * BS_sd

# Simple slopes for sexual objectification frequency at each benevolent sexism value.
HC3_BS_trends <- emtrends(mod3,
                             specs = ~ BS_c,
                             var = "SO_c",
                             at = list(BS_c = BS_values),
                             vcov. = vcovHC(mod3, type = "HC3"))

# Building a data frame of the simple slopes
HC3_simple_slopes_df <- summary(HC3_BS_trends,
  infer = c(TRUE, TRUE),
  null = 0) |> 
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(BS_level = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")) |>
  select(BS_level, SO_c.trend, SE, df, t.ratio, p.value, lower.CL, upper.CL)

## Turning the simple slopes dataframe into a table
HC3_simple_slopes_table <- gt(HC3_simple_slopes_df) |> 
  cols_label(BS_level = "Benevolent Sexism",
             SO_c.trend = "Estimate",
             lower.CL = "Lower 95% CI",
             upper.CL = "Upper 95% CI",
             t.ratio = "t",
             p.value = "p") |> 
fmt_number(columns = c(SO_c.trend, SE, t.ratio, lower.CL, upper.CL), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt(columns = p.value,
      fns = \(x) scales::pvalue(x, accuracy = 0.001, add_p = FALSE)) |>
  cols_move(columns = c(lower.CL, upper.CL),
    after = SE) |> 
  tab_header(title = "Simple Effects of Sexual Objectication Frequency Across Levels of Benevolent Sexism")

# Generating predicted outcomes to prepare visualization
HC3_predictions <- ggpredict(mod3,
  terms = c("SO_c", "BS_c [meansd]"), # Specifying the three levels of benevolent sexism
  vcov.fun = sandwich::vcovHC,
  vcov.type = "HC3")

# Un-centering the mean to make scale values more interpretable
predictions_df <- as.data.frame(HC3_predictions) |> 
  mutate(SO_original = x + m_SO,
    BS_original = as.numeric(as.character(group)) + m_BS,
    predicted_original = predicted + m_PSA,
    conf.low_original = conf.low + m_PSA,
    conf.high_original = conf.high + m_PSA)

# Creating plot
HC3_plot <- ggplot(predictions_df,
         aes(x = SO_original, y = predicted_original,
             colour = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low_original, ymax = conf.high_original),
    alpha = 0.15,
    colour = NA) +
  scale_colour_discrete(labels = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")) +
  scale_fill_discrete(labels = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "Sexual Objectification Experience Frequency",
    y = "Predicted Safety Anxiety",
    colour = "Benevolent Sexism",
    fill = "Benevolent Sexism",
    title = "Simple Slopes of Objectification Frequency at Levels of Benevolent Sexism")
```

Consistent with the zero-order correlation results, the HC3-adjusted regression results indicated that sexual objectification frequency was positively associated with personal safety anxiety (*b* = `r round(coefficient_results$estimate[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c"], 2)`, *SE* = `r round(coefficient_results$std.error[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c"], 2)`, 95% CI \[`r sprintf("%.2f", coefficient_results$conf.low[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", coefficient_results$conf.high[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c"])`\], *p* `r ifelse(coefficient_results$p.value[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", sprintf("%.3f", coefficient_results$p.value[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c"])))`). This suggests that, at the average level of benevolent sexism, a one-point increase in sexual objectification frequency was associated with an estimated `r sprintf("%.2f", coefficient_results$estimate[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c"])`-point increase in personal safety anxiety.

In contrast, the main effect of benevolent sexism was not statistically significant (*b* = `r round(coefficient_results$estimate[coefficient_results$term == "BS_c"], 2)`, *SE* = `r round(coefficient_results$std.error[coefficient_results$term == "BS_c"], 2)`, 95% CI \[`r sprintf("%.2f", coefficient_results$conf.low[coefficient_results$term == "BS_c"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", coefficient_results$conf.high[coefficient_results$term == "BS_c"])`\], *p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", coefficient_results$p.value[coefficient_results$term == "BS_c"])`). More importantly, the interaction between sexual objectification frequency and benevolent sexism was also non-significant (*b* = `r round(coefficient_results$estimate[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c:BS_c"], 2)`, *SE* = `r round(coefficient_results$std.error[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c:BS_c"], 2)`, 95% CI \[`r sprintf("%.2f", coefficient_results$conf.low[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c:BS_c"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", coefficient_results$conf.high[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c:BS_c"])`\], *p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", coefficient_results$p.value[coefficient_results$term == "SO_c:BS_c"])`). Additionally, the positive interaction estimate was directionally opposed with the hypothesized moderating effect. As its confidence interval included zero, however, there remains substantial uncertainty regarding the presence and magnitude of moderation.

```{r}
coefficient_results |>
  mutate(term = dplyr::recode(term,
                              "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
                              "SO_c" = "Sexual Objectification Experience Frequency",
                              "BS_c" = "Benevolent Sexism",
                              "SO_c:BS_c" = "Sexual Objectification × Benevolent Sexism")) |>
  select(term,
         estimate,
         std.error,
         conf.low,
         conf.high,
         p.value) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(term = "Predictor",
             estimate = "Estimate",
             std.error = "SE",
             conf.low = "95% CI lower",
             conf.high = "95% CI upper",
             p.value = "p") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(
    estimate,
    std.error,
    conf.low,
    conf.high),
    decimals = 3) |>
  fmt(columns = p.value,
      fns = function(x) {
        ifelse(
          x < .001,
          "< .001",
          sprintf("%.3f", x))}) |> 
  tab_header(title = "Interaction Model Results with HC3 Estimator")
```
Simple slopes were subsequently examined to clarify the conditional associations between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety at different levels of benevolent sexism. The conditional association was positive and statistically significant at average levels (*b* = `r round(HC3_simple_slopes_df$SO_c.trend[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "Mean"], 2)`, *SE* = `r round(HC3_simple_slopes_df$SE[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "Mean"], 2)`, 95% CI \[`r sprintf("%.2f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$lower.CL[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "Mean"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$upper.CL[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "Mean"])`\], *p* `r ifelse(HC3_simple_slopes_df$p.value[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "Mean"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", sprintf("%.3f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$p.value[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "Mean"])))`) and high levels of benevolent sexism (*b* = `r round(HC3_simple_slopes_df$SO_c.trend[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "+1 SD"], 2)`, *SE* = `r round(HC3_simple_slopes_df$SE[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "+1 SD"], 2)`, 95% CI \[`r sprintf("%.2f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$lower.CL[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "+1 SD"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$upper.CL[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "+1 SD"])`\], *p* `r ifelse(HC3_simple_slopes_df$p.value[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "+1 SD"] < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", sprintf("%.3f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$p.value[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "+1 SD"])))`), but not at low levels (*b* = `r round(HC3_simple_slopes_df$SO_c.trend[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "-1 SD"], 2)`, *SE* = `r round(HC3_simple_slopes_df$SE[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "-1 SD"], 2)`, 95% CI \[`r sprintf("%.2f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$lower.CL[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "-1 SD"])`, `r sprintf("%.2f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$upper.CL[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "-1 SD"])`\], *p* = `r sprintf("%.3f", HC3_simple_slopes_df$p.value[HC3_simple_slopes_df$BS_level == "-1 SD"])`). 

Although these estimates suggest that the association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety was numerically stronger at higher levels of benevolent sexism, the non-significant interaction indicates that the differences between these slopes cannot be confidently distinguished from sampling variability. The wide confidence intervals further emphasize the uncertainty of these estimates. Therefore, the simple slopes trends should not be interpreted as evidence that benevolent sexism significantly moderates the association.

```{r}
HC3_simple_slopes_table

HC3_plot
```

## Discussion
The present study examined the association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety, with particular attention to whether benevolent sexism influenced the strength of this relationship. Overall, the findings provide support for the association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety, but did not establish a significant moderating role of benevolent sexism. 

Consistent with the first hypothesis, more frequent experiences of sexual objectification were significantly associated with greater personal safety anxiety. This finding aligns with objectification theory and previous research demonstrating that sexually objectifying experiences can contribute to women's concerns about personal safety and physical vulnerability (Calogero et al., 2021). The observed association suggests that women who experience more frequent objectifying treatment may also experience greater apprehension and vigilance concerning potential threats to their personal safety. Although the proportion of variance explained was relatively modest, the finding reinforces the relevance of examining safety-related concerns as one potential consequence of everyday objectification.

The findings concerning the moderating role of benevolent sexism were less conclusive. Firstly, this variable was not independently associated with personal safety anxiety. These findings suggest that endorsement of benevolent sexist attitudes, at least as measured in the present sample, may not independently account for substantial differences in women's personal safety anxiety once experiences of sexual objectification frequency are considered. Similarly, the hypothesized moderating effect was not statistically supported. Although the interaction coefficient was positive and the simple slopes increased numerically across levels of benevolent sexism, the interaction confidence interval included zero. Consequently, the apparent differences between the simple slopes should be interpreted cautiously: The results do not provide sufficient evidence to conclude that women who endorse stronger benevolent sexist beliefs experience a stronger association between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety. Nevertheless, the unexpected direction of the (non-significant) moderating effect underscores the need for further research to clarify the mechanisms underlying this relationship and identify potentially relevant covariates.

Importantly, these findings do not necessarily establish that benevolent sexism is irrelevant to women's experiences of personal safety. Rather, they suggest that the specific moderating relationship examined here was not reliably demonstrated. It is possible that benevolent sexism influences other aspects of women's interpretations of gendered experiences, or that its relationship with personal safety anxiety depends on additional contextual or individual factors not considered in the current models. It is also possible that a different analytic model may more accurately describe the relationships between these variables. For instance, a study by Hammond and colleagues (2024) suggested that when women experience greater vulnerability, threat, or reduced personal control, benevolent sexism may become more psychologically appealing to endorse because it offers an ideological framework emphasizing protection, security, and relational dependence. Thus, benevolent sexism may instead be better positioned as a response to safety anxiety, rather than as a moderator.

#### Limitations and Future Directions
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, the observational nature of the data prevents causal conclusions. Although sexual objectification frequency was positively associated with personal safety anxiety, the analyses cannot establish whether objectifying experiences produce greater safety anxiety or whether other factors contribute to both. Second, the sample was relatively young and university-educated, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to women in other age groups and social contexts. Third, the measure of sexual objectification frequency was created by combining select measures from three distinct validated scales. Although the internal reliability in the current sample was high, thorough examination of the scale's other psychometric properties would provide better confidence in its validity and reliability. Fourth, the models explained a relatively small proportion of the variance in personal safety anxiety, suggesting that additional psychological, interpersonal, and contextual factors should be integrated into a model predicting women's safety-related concerns. Finally, the sample size may have limited statistical power to detect relatively small moderation effects. Interaction effects are often more difficult to detect than main effects, and the confidence interval surrounding the interaction estimate remained relatively wide. In turn, a larger sample size may be better positioned to detect small interaction effects.

Future research could examine additional factors that may influence the relationship between sexual objectification frequency and personal safety anxiety, including previous experiences of harassment or general sexism, perceived environmental safety (e.g., neighbourhood safety statistics), individual differences in threat appraisal and resilience, and various demographic characteristics. A different measure of sexual objectification that captures its impact rather than frequency may be warranted. Re-testing the proposed interaction model in an age-diverse, non-university sample would provide additional valuable context regarding the nature of the results. Further investigation of the psychometric properties of all three scales may also help clarify whether measurement limitations contributed to the nonsignificant moderation findings. Longitudinal research could additionally provide greater insight into the temporal and causal relationships between objectifying experiences, safety-related concerns, and gender-role beliefs.

#### Conclusion
Overall, the present findings reinforce the importance of considering personal safety anxiety as a psychological correlate of women's experiences of sexual objectification frequency. Although benevolent sexism was theoretically relevant to the proposed relationship, the current analyses did not provide sufficient evidence that it significantly moderates this association. The findings highlight the importance of transparent model comparison and cautious interpretation in psychological research.

```{r}
                          at = list(BS_c = BS_values),
                          vcov. = vcovHC(mod3_sensitivity, type = "HC3"))

# Building a data frame of the simple slopes
Sensitivity_simple_slopes_df <- summary(Sensitivity_BS_trends,
                                infer = c(TRUE, TRUE),
                                null = 0) |> 
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(BS_level = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")) |>
  select(BS_level, SO_c.trend, SE, df, t.ratio, p.value, lower.CL, upper.CL)

## Turning the simple slopes dataframe into a table
Sensitivity_simple_slopes_table <- gt(Sensitivity_simple_slopes_df) |> 
  cols_label(BS_level = "Benevolent Sexism",
             SO_c.trend = "Estimate",
             lower.CL = "Lower 95% CI",
             upper.CL = "Upper 95% CI",
             t.ratio = "t",
             p.value = "p") |> 
  fmt_number(columns = c(SO_c.trend, SE, t.ratio, lower.CL, upper.CL), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt(columns = p.value,
      fns = \(x) scales::pvalue(x, accuracy = 0.001, add_p = FALSE)) |>
  cols_move(columns = c(lower.CL, upper.CL),
            after = SE) |> 
  tab_header(title = "Simple Effects of Sexual Objectification Frequency Across Levels of Benevolent Sexism")

# Generating predicted outcomes to prepare visualization
Sensitivity_predictions <- ggpredict(mod3_sensitivity,
                             terms = c("SO_c", "BS_c [meansd]"), # Specifying the three levels of benevolent sexism
                             vcov.fun = sandwich::vcovHC,
                             vcov.type = "HC3")

# Un-centering the mean to make scale values more interpretable
Sensitivity_predictions_df <- as.data.frame(Sensitivity_predictions) |> 
  mutate(SO_original = x + m_SO,
         BS_original = as.numeric(as.character(group)) + m_BS,
         predicted_original = predicted + m_PSA,
         conf.low_original = conf.low + m_PSA,
         conf.high_original = conf.high + m_PSA)

# Creating plot
Sensitivity_plot <- ggplot(Sensitivity_predictions_df,
                   aes(x = SO_original, y = predicted_original,
                       colour = group, fill = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low_original, ymax = conf.high_original),
              alpha = 0.15,
              colour = NA) +
  scale_colour_discrete(labels = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")) +
  scale_fill_discrete(labels = c("-1 SD", "Mean", "+1 SD")) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "Sexual Objectification Experience Frequency",
       y = "Predicted Safety Anxiety",
       colour = "Benevolent Sexism",
       fill = "Benevolent Sexism",
       title = "Simple Slopes of Objectification Frequency at Levels of Benevolent Sexism")

Sensitivity_simple_slopes_table
Sensitivity_plot
```
